title: Six pairs
hook: calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, in body and in mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, sobhana, the beautiful factors: faith, mindfulness, conscience, concern, an open hand, a friendly face, balance. Your line: the beautiful. Whose beautiful moment did you catch? Day one thousand seventy-nine.

Cold dough tears. Push a rolling pin across it straight from the fridge and it cracks at the edges, fights back, springs into its old shape. Leave the same dough on the counter for a while and it rolls out smooth, takes any shape, does what the hands ask. Nothing was added. It just softened. Today the manual finishes its list of the beautiful factors present in every beautiful moment, with six qualities that sound a lot like warm dough.

The six come in pairs, and every pair has the same shape: one of the body, one of the mind. Tranquility, passaddhi: calm, the settling of agitation. Lightness, lahuta: not heavy, not dragging. Softness, muduta: not rigid, not stubborn. Workability, kammannata: fit for work, ready to be used. Proficiency, pagunnata: skill, a mind that runs well. And straightness, ujukata: not crooked, without twists or tricks. A note on body. In the Abhidhamma, the body in these pairs means the cluster of mental factors, the mind's own small body, not flesh and bone. Still, some teachers point out that these qualities can be felt physically too, in shoulders that drop, a jaw that lets go. The suttas have a picture for a mind like this. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes gold being refined. Iron, copper, tin, lead and silver are worked out of it, and then the gold is pliant, workable and bright, ready for whatever ornament the goldsmith has in mind. So too, he says, a mind freed of its impurities is pliant, workable and luminous. Straightness has a Dhammapada verse of its own, in Max Müller's words: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back." Here is the useful part. In the manual, these qualities aren't a prize at the end of a long road. They are counted in every beautiful moment. Whenever a moment of kindness or clear seeing happens, some softness and workability are already in it. On this account, a stiff, stubborn mood can't arise in the same moment as real generosity. One is cold dough. The other rolls.
screen: `ONE OF THE BODY, ONE OF THE MIND.` · `GOLD MADE PLIANT AND BRIGHT.` · `THE FLETCHER STRAIGHTENS THE ARROW.` · then, large: `COLD DOUGH, OR DOUGH THAT ROLLS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: feel the body soften. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then go looking for stiffness: the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, the space between the eyebrows. Don't force anything to relax. Just rest attention there and let the next out-breath be a little longer. See if the place softens on its own, the way dough does on a counter. Then check the mind the same way. Is there a thought it's gripping stiffly? Let it be held a little more lightly. The bell holds the time.
Six pairs. Calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, each in the body of mental factors and in the mind. Today's word.
Your line: soft and workable. Today, before a hard conversation or a hard task, check for cold dough in the jaw, the shoulders, the hands. Let one of them soften first. Day one thousand seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the six pairs as part of the beautiful factors, and some meditation teachers point to tranquility, lightness and pliancy of body and mind as signs that practice is settling.

original.note: Pali passaddhi: tranquility, the first of the six pairs.

trapdoor: what you thought: a calm mind is just a quiet one.
what it means: calm comes with lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness.
what a scholar hears: the manual lists each quality twice, as kaya, the body of mental factors, and as citta, consciousness itself.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.23 (Upakkilesa Sutta): gold freed of five impurities
Abhidhammattha Sangaha, ch. 2 (the six pairs among the beautiful universals)

notes: The six pairs (kaya- and citta-: passaddhi, lahuta, muduta, kammannata, pagunnata, ujukata) are from Abhidhammattha Sangaha ch. 2. 'kaya' here is the 'mental body', the aggregate of mental factors, per the standard commentarial reading. Confirm.

AN 5.23 paraphrased: gold with five impurities (iron, copper, tin, lead, silver) is not pliant or workable; freed of them it is; likewise the mind freed of the five hindrances is 'pliant, workable and luminous'. Confirm the exact list of metals.
'some teachers point out that these qualities can be felt physically' is deliberately hedged.
'a stiff, stubborn mood and a moment of real generosity don't share a moment' is the writer's inference from the pairs being universal to beautiful consciousness; confirm it is fair.
The dough image is everyday, not a tradition claim.
Editor: rewrote the unclear line 'don't share a moment' as 'can't arise in the same moment'.
